title: Registration and device-enrollment data can identify the homeowner
description: The flow carries account-registration details and enrolled camera/sensor identifiers to the Home Hub. These data can directly identify the homeowner or make them identifiable when linked to a home address, account, or device inventory.
assumptions: Assumes the registration payload includes personal data such as name, email, phone number, address, account identifier, or uniquely assigned device identifiers tied to the household.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicability of Identifiability to ExternalEntity->Process flows, not the detailed subtree.

title: Enrollment traffic can link multiple devices and the account to the same household
description: By enrolling several cameras and sensors through one registration flow, the Home Hub can associate all submitted device identifiers and account details with a single homeowner and household. This enables linking across devices and future interactions.
assumptions: Assumes device serial numbers, MAC addresses, model identifiers, or setup tokens are transmitted together with account-registration data.
uncertainty_note: Detailed tree-node id is approximate; retrieved context supports Linkability as applicable on this flow type but does not provide the exact subtree.

title: The registration flow may disclose sensitive household and security information
description: Enrollment of cameras and sensors reveals the existence, type, and number of monitoring devices in the home. This can disclose private facts about the household's layout, occupancy concerns, security posture, or presence of specific rooms or assets.
assumptions: Assumes the flow includes device types, locations, names, or metadata beyond a minimal opaque enrollment token.
uncertainty_note: Exact subtree is inferred from general LINDDUN disclosure threats; the KB excerpt only establishes that Disclosure applies to this interaction type.

title: The homeowner may be unable to prove or contest what was registered or enrolled
description: If the Home Hub does not provide verifiable receipts, timestamps, or auditable confirmation of account creation and device enrollment, the homeowner may later be unable to demonstrate which devices were enrolled, when enrollment occurred, or whether consented registration details were altered.
assumptions: Assumes enrollment events are not strongly logged or user-visible confirmations are incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Applicability is plausible for this flow, but depends on whether the system relies on enrollment records for dispute resolution.

title: The homeowner may lack awareness of what personal and device data are collected during setup
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the Home Hub may collect more data than the homeowner expects, such as persistent device identifiers, network metadata, location hints, or household composition indicators. If setup UX does not clearly explain this, users may not understand the privacy impact.
assumptions: Assumes the setup process does not fully and clearly communicate categories, purposes, retention, and recipients of collected data.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the threat is grounded in unawareness during collection on this flow.

title: Registration and enrollment may collect data without valid or sufficiently specific consent
description: If the Home Hub requests broad acceptance during setup without granular choices, the homeowner may be unable to meaningfully consent to collection and processing of account details, device identifiers, and household-security metadata associated with enrollment.
assumptions: Assumes consent is the legal basis or that notice/choice obligations apply, and that setup bundles multiple purposes together.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the product's legal basis and consent design; if another lawful basis applies and transparency obligations are met, this threat may be less applicable.

title: Temporary access code can be linked to a specific guest or visit
description: If the Home Hub receives a temporary access code that is unique per guest, booking, or visit window, the code entry event can be linked to a particular guest and correlated with other events such as door unlocks, timestamps, or camera/log records. This enables linking multiple actions or sessions to the same data subject.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are unique or sufficiently distinctive and that the Home Hub stores or exposes associated event logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; exact sub-node may vary depending on the project’s threat-tree version.

title: Temporary access code may identify the guest directly or indirectly
description: The access code submission may identify a guest if the code is assigned to a named individual, reservation, phone number, or household visitor record. Even if the code itself is pseudonymous, the Home Hub may be able to resolve it to a specific person, making the incoming flow identifying.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub or connected backend can map temporary codes to guest identities or guest records.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node granularity is approximate because the retrieved context only confirms applicability at flow/source level for ExternalEntity→Process.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having entered the code
description: If the Home Hub logs code entry attempts together with timestamps and code values or resolved guest identifiers, the resulting records can serve as evidence that a particular guest attempted or performed an unlock action. This creates a non-repudiation threat from a privacy perspective because the guest may later be unable to plausibly deny participation.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub keeps audit logs of code entry attempts and can associate them with a guest or temporary credential.
uncertainty_note: Sub-node selected by best judgement; exact numbering may differ across LINDDUN Pro materials.

title: Observation of code-entry interaction can reveal guest participation
description: An observer who can monitor the communication or visible interaction with the Home Hub may infer that a guest is currently present and attempting entry, even without learning the code itself. The mere existence and timing of this flow can reveal the guest’s involvement with the household or visit.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe the interaction channel, device state changes, or immediate system responses.
uncertainty_note: Grounded in LINDDUN detecting guidance about observed communication and system responses; exact sub-node id is approximate.

title: Code entry discloses presence and visit timing information
description: The temporary access code flow discloses personal data beyond the credential itself, notably that a guest is at the door at a particular time and is authorized or attempting to gain access. If logged or exposed to other components, this can reveal visit patterns and occupancy-related personal information.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub processes, logs, or forwards metadata such as timestamps, success/failure, or associated guest records.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node is approximate; disclosure here includes metadata and inferred personal information, not only the raw code.

title: Guest may be unaware how code-entry data is processed
description: The guest may not understand what happens to the temporary access code and related metadata after entry—such as whether attempts are logged, how long records are retained, whether failed attempts are monitored, or whether data is shared with homeowners or service providers. This creates an unawareness threat around the processing of the flow.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly inform guests about logging, retention, sharing, and monitoring of access-code events.
uncertainty_note: Applicable as an unawareness threat on this flow, but exact node numbering is based on best judgement.

title: Processing of guest access-code data may lack valid consent or another legal basis
description: The Home Hub processes the guest’s temporary access code and associated metadata to authenticate entry. If the guest has not been properly informed or has not provided valid consent where required, or if another appropriate legal basis and transparency obligations are not satisfied, this flow may be non-compliant with privacy requirements.
assumptions: Assumes applicable law requires transparency and a valid legal basis for processing guest access-event data.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction and deployment context; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Event log enables linkage of household activity over time
description: Writing motion, door, and sensor events into a persistent local log creates a longitudinal record that can be linked into occupancy patterns, routines, and correlations between different sensors within the same home.
assumptions: The local event log retains per-event timestamps and sensor identifiers long enough to reconstruct behavior patterns.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgment because the retrieved context only confirms applicability by threat type, not detailed node ids.

title: Local event log can identify residents through behavioral signatures
description: Even if the log does not store explicit names, repeated motion/door/sensor events may reveal distinctive behavioral patterns that identify or single out household members or visitors.
assumptions: Events are sufficiently granular and attributable to locations/devices so that behavior patterns can be distinguished.
uncertainty_note: Identification may depend on granularity and household size; detailed threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Home Hub may be unable to prove what events were actually logged
description: If writes from the Home Hub to the local event log lack integrity protection, timestamps, or audit evidence, the system may later be unable to demonstrate whether a specific sensor event was recorded, omitted, or altered, undermining accountability around personal-event processing.
assumptions: The flow or resulting log entries do not include strong write-audit mechanisms or tamper-evident logging.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation is included by the mapping table, but applicability depends on whether accountability for event logging is a system requirement.

title: Event log reveals sensitive inferences about presence and habits
description: Stored motion, door, and sensor events can disclose when occupants are home, asleep, away, or following particular routines, exposing private facts about daily life.
assumptions: The event types and timestamps are accessible to some actor or component beyond the immediate sensing function.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate; disclosure clearly applies to this persistent event log.

title: Persistent local logging may exceed data minimization needs
description: Recording all motion, door, and sensor events in a local event log may collect or retain more personal data than necessary for the immediate home-automation purpose, especially if fine-grained timestamps and long retention are used.
assumptions: The system logs all raw events and retains them beyond the shortest operational need.
uncertainty_note: Detectability in LINDDUN Pro can overlap with observability/inference concerns; this entry uses the common interpretation that the data subject's activities become readily detectable from the stored events.

title: Residents may be unaware that detailed sensor events are being logged
description: Because the Home Hub silently writes sensor activity to a local event log, occupants or visitors may not understand that their movements and interactions are persistently recorded.
assumptions: The system does not provide clear notice or local transparency about event logging.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is plausible for this flow, but depends on the product's notice and UI design.

title: Local event logging may violate consent or purpose limitations
description: If motion, door, and sensor events are logged without valid consent, without another lawful basis, or reused beyond the original home-automation purpose, the logging operation may be non-compliant with privacy requirements.
assumptions: Applicable policy or law requires consent, purpose limitation, retention limits, or similar controls for this household event data.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on jurisdiction, deployment context, and product policy; tree-node id is approximate.

title: Upload metadata can link clips to a specific household and routine
description: When the Home Hub uploads recorded camera clips, the flow is likely to include stable identifiers and metadata such as device ID, account ID, camera ID, timestamps, and network/account context. These can allow the cloud side or anyone with access to the flow/storage context to link multiple uploads to the same home, infer occupancy patterns, and correlate events over time.
assumptions: Assumes uploaded clips carry persistent identifiers or rich metadata beyond raw video bytes.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement because the retrieved context confirms applicability of Linkability to Process->DataStore flows but does not provide the detailed subtree ids.

title: Recorded clips and metadata can identify residents or visitors
description: Video clips uploaded from the Home Hub may contain faces, voices, interiors, addresses, or other contextual details. Even if direct identifiers are absent, the content and associated metadata can identify household members, visitors, or the specific residence.
assumptions: Assumes the recorded clips contain recognizable people or location-specific context, which is typical for home security video.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node id is inferred from general LINDDUN identifiability concepts; retrieved context does not include subtree detail.

title: Cloud upload exposes highly sensitive private activities
description: Uploading home camera recordings to cloud storage can disclose intimate details of life inside or around the home, including presence at home, daily routines, visitors, possessions, and potentially special-category data visible in footage. The transfer itself expands exposure beyond the local environment.
assumptions: Assumes clips cover private household spaces or entrances and are accessible to cloud-side systems or personnel under some conditions.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort due to missing detailed subtree mapping in the provided context.

title: Cloud storage may be unaware of collection context and retention expectations
description: Once clips are uploaded into Cloud Video Storage, the datastore may lack sufficient context about why each clip was recorded, what notice was given to data subjects, applicable retention limits, or whether consent/other legal basis covers cloud storage. This can lead to processing beyond the data subjects' reasonable expectations.
assumptions: Assumes context such as purpose, notice state, retention policy, or legal basis is not fully bound to each uploaded clip.
uncertainty_note: Applicability is plausible for this flow, but exact unawareness subtree id is inferred rather than cited from the retrieved context.

title: Uploading home video to cloud may violate data minimization or purpose/retention constraints
description: Sending full recorded clips to cloud storage may collect and retain more personal data than necessary for the stated purpose, especially if continuous or broad recordings are uploaded, if bystanders are captured, or if clips are kept longer than needed. This creates risk of non-compliance with minimization, purpose limitation, transparency, and storage-limitation obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the system uploads full clips and stores them centrally rather than minimizing content, duration, or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance is strongly plausible, but depends on actual legal basis, notices, retention settings, and minimization controls.

title: Real-time motion alerts may disclose occupancy/activity patterns beyond what is necessary
description: The Home Hub forwards a real-time motion alert to the mobile app backend. Motion alerts constitute personal data because they reveal presence, movement, and potentially occupancy routines inside a home. This flow creates a data-disclosure risk if the alert contains more detail than needed for backend processing, or if sending every event in real time unnecessarily exposes fine-grained behavioral patterns to another system component.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert is linked or linkable to a household, device, account, or location, and that the backend does not strictly require all included fields or full event granularity.

title: Repeated motion-alert transmissions can enable linkage of events to a specific household or user profile
description: A stream of real-time motion alerts sent from the Home Hub to the backend can be correlated over time using stable identifiers, device metadata, account references, timestamps, or network-level attributes. This may allow the backend or downstream recipients to link separate events into a detailed profile of one household's routines and behavior.
assumptions: Assumes alerts carry persistent identifiers or sufficiently consistent metadata to associate multiple events with the same home, device, or account.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on general LINDDUN linkage categories; exact subnode naming may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Motion-alert content and metadata may allow identification of residents or a specific home
description: Even if the payload does not explicitly name a person, a real-time motion alert may include device IDs, account IDs, address-linked hub identifiers, or precise timestamps that make the household or residents identifiable. In a smart-home context, identifying the home often effectively identifies the occupants.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can associate hub/device identifiers with customer records, service addresses, or user accounts.
uncertainty_note: Exact I-subnode may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions; this is a best-fit identification node.

title: Backend can infer sensitive occupancy routines from incoming motion alerts
description: By receiving real-time motion alerts, the mobile app backend can derive when occupants are home, asleep, away, or following recurring routines. These inferences may go beyond the user's expectations if the backend only ostensibly handles alert delivery but can also analyze behavioral patterns.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores, aggregates, or analyzes alerts over time rather than treating them as transient relay messages only.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is a best-fit generic detectability/inference node; exact numbering may vary.

title: Forwarding motion alerts to the backend may be incompatible with data-minimization or purpose-limitation expectations
description: Sending real-time motion events from the Home Hub to the mobile app backend may exceed what users reasonably expect if the backend's role could be fulfilled with less detailed, less frequent, or more local processing. This creates a non-compliance risk under privacy principles such as data minimization, necessity, and purpose limitation.
assumptions: Assumes no clearly established necessity for transmitting full real-time motion-event data to the backend, or that user notice/consent does not specifically cover this processing.
uncertainty_note: Compliance assessment depends on system purpose, legal basis, and transparency details not provided here.

title: Notification content can link the event to a specific household or resident
description: A motion-detected push notification sent from the backend to the homeowner's phone may contain identifiers such as device name, address context, room/camera label, or account-specific metadata. If observed by intermediaries, OS notification services, or someone with access to the phone lock screen, the message can be linked to a particular home or resident.
assumptions: Assumes the notification payload includes identifiable context beyond a generic alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicability of L to Process->ExternalEntity flows, not the detailed subtree.

title: Repeated motion alerts enable inference of occupancy patterns
description: Even if the notification content is minimal, the timing and frequency of motion-detected notifications can reveal when people are home, awake, away, or moving through the property. This allows inference of behavioral routines from the flow itself.
assumptions: Assumes notifications are generated with enough regularity that timing patterns are observable by the recipient device, platform provider, or anyone viewing notification history.
uncertainty_note: Detailed tree-node id is approximate; inference from event timing is the main concern.

title: Notification discloses sensitive home-security event information to unintended viewers
description: A motion-detected alert is privacy-sensitive because it reveals activity at the home. If the notification is displayed on a lock screen, wearable, shared device, or exposed through push-service infrastructure, sensitive information about the household may be disclosed to parties other than the intended homeowner.
assumptions: Assumes notification previews or metadata are visible outside the app's protected context.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the core issue is unauthorized disclosure of event information on this outbound flow.

title: Homeowner may be unaware that motion events are pushed via third-party notification channels
description: The backend's delivery of motion alerts may rely on mobile push ecosystems and expose event metadata outside the core service. If users are not clearly informed about what data is included in notifications, where it is processed, and how lock-screen visibility works, they may lack awareness of this privacy-relevant processing.
assumptions: Assumes the service uses standard mobile push providers and user notice/controls are limited or unclear.
uncertainty_note: This is a usability/awareness threat tied to the flow, but exact subtree mapping is based on best judgement.

title: Pushing detailed motion notifications may exceed user consent or configured privacy preferences
description: If the backend sends detailed motion-detected notifications by default, or continues after the user has disabled previews, changed alert preferences, or not consented to this use of event data, the flow may violate consent and choice expectations. This is especially relevant if notifications include rich contextual details.
assumptions: Assumes notification settings, consent choices, or privacy preferences exist or are expected for this feature.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the product's consent and preference model; included because outbound event notifications commonly require user-configurable privacy choices.

title: Shared analytics may still enable linkage to individual users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend may disclose stable device, account, cohort, timestamp, or event dimensions that allow the cloud analytics vendor to link records across uploads or combine them with other datasets, re-identifying or singling out users/devices.
assumptions: Assumes the aggregation is not strongly privacy-preserving and that the vendor can access repeated submissions or auxiliary data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types for Process->ExternalEntity, not detailed node ids.

title: Analytics payload may reveal sensitive inferences about user behavior
description: Even aggregated usage analytics can expose interests, routines, health, work patterns, location habits, or other behavioral characteristics when broken down by feature, time, geography, or device segment. Sending such analytics to the vendor may therefore disclose information beyond what users expect.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics dimensions are sufficiently granular to support inference about individuals or small groups.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node id is approximate.

title: Transfer to third-party analytics vendor may occur without adequate user awareness
description: Users may not realize that their app usage data, even in aggregated form, is shared with an external analytics vendor. If notices are unclear or incomplete, the flow creates a detectability/transparency risk because the existence, scope, or recipient of the disclosure is not readily apparent to data subjects.
assumptions: Assumes privacy notices or in-app disclosures do not clearly explain this vendor sharing.
uncertainty_note: Using detectability in the LINDDUN sense of insufficient transparency/awareness; node id is approximate.

title: Users may lack sufficient control over disclosure of analytics data to the vendor
description: If the backend sends analytics to the cloud vendor by default without a meaningful opt-out, consent choice, or granular controls, users may be unable to decide whether their usage data is disclosed to this third party.
assumptions: Assumes analytics sharing is enabled by default or controls are absent, bundled, or ineffective.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate.

title: Secondary use by analytics vendor may exceed the original purpose
description: Once transferred, aggregated analytics may be used by the vendor for its own service improvement, benchmarking, model training, profiling, or cross-customer analytics, making the eventual use of the data insufficiently constrained or predictable for users.
assumptions: Assumes contractual and technical purpose limitation controls are weak or absent.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate.

title: Sharing analytics with external vendor may violate consent, minimization, or cross-border requirements
description: This disclosure may be non-compliant if the analytics data is personal data under applicable law, if aggregation is insufficient for anonymization, if the transfer lacks a valid legal basis, if retention/purpose limits are not enforced, or if international transfer obligations are unmet.
assumptions: Assumes at least some jurisdictions or policies treat the shared analytics as regulated personal data or pseudonymous data.
uncertainty_note: Detailed node id is approximate and depends on jurisdiction, contract terms, and actual anonymization strength.

title: Backend can link retrieved video clips to a specific homeowner account
description: When P2 retrieves a stored clip from DS2 for playback, the retrieval request and returned clip can be associated with the authenticated homeowner account, device/session identifiers, timestamps, and camera identifiers. This enables linking viewing events and video content to the same individual across sessions, revealing behavior patterns such as presence at home or monitoring habits.
assumptions: P2 has access to account identifiers and metadata needed to select the requested clip, and logs or internal state may preserve these associations.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgment; the retrieved context did not include a specific linkability node id.

title: Retrieved clip may identify residents, visitors, or household routines
description: The video clip returned to P2 can contain faces, voices, location cues, timestamps, and household activity. Processing this clip at the backend can directly identify the homeowner or other individuals captured in the footage, especially when combined with account and camera metadata already available to P2.
assumptions: Stored clips contain personal data and P2 can access associated metadata such as account, camera, and time information.
uncertainty_note: Specific identifiability subtree id is selected by best judgment because no exact node id was provided in the retrieved context.

title: Backend retrieval exposes sensitive information about home occupancy and activities
description: By receiving the clip from DS2, P2 processes footage and metadata that can disclose whether people are home, when they arrive or leave, daily routines, visitors, and interior details of the residence. Even if the clip is requested for legitimate playback, the backend's access to the content creates a disclosure risk if access controls, segregation, or handling are insufficient.
assumptions: P2 can access raw clip content or rich metadata rather than only opaque encrypted blobs.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure subtree id is selected by best judgment; exact node id not present in the retrieved context.

title: Playback retrieval reveals that a homeowner is interested in a specific event or time window
description: The act of retrieving a particular stored clip can itself disclose information: which camera was checked, what time period was reviewed, and that the homeowner considered that event noteworthy. This can reveal concerns, routines, absences, or incidents even apart from the clip contents.
assumptions: P2 observes clip-selection metadata, request timing, and camera identifiers, and may log or analyze playback requests.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgment; no exact detectability node id was included in the retrieved context.

title: Secondary backend use of retrieved clips may exceed the homeowner's expectations
description: A clip retrieved for immediate playback could also be reused by P2 for analytics, model training, employee review, troubleshooting, or law-enforcement response without the homeowner clearly understanding that these additional uses occur. The retrieval step therefore creates a risk that processing purposes are broader than the user's expectations.
assumptions: The service architecture allows backend-side access to clip contents or metadata beyond simple pass-through delivery.
uncertainty_note: Specific unawareness subtree id is selected by best judgment because the retrieved context did not provide one.

title: Retrieved video and playback metadata may be retained longer than necessary
description: Once P2 retrieves the clip from DS2, the backend may cache the video, create temporary copies, or retain playback/access logs. If these artifacts are kept beyond what is necessary for playback or operational needs, the system violates the storage limitation principle.
assumptions: P2 creates transient or persistent copies, caches, or logs during retrieval and playback handling.
